lesson.title: Load, Select, Filter, Clean and Group CSV Data with Pandas
lesson.goal: load a CSV with pandas, then select, filter, clean and group the data

sources.title: Load, Select, Filter, Clean and Group CSV Data with Pandas

steps.title: Install pandas and load CSV
steps.instructions: Run `uv init .` and `uv add pandas` (or `pip install pandas`), download orders.csv from https://github.com/techwithtim/PanadasTutorial into the folder, then in main.py import pandas as pd, load it with pd.read_csv('orders.csv') and print(df). Run `uv run main.py` to see the DataFrame summary line like [40 rows x 9 columns].

targets.caption: Import pandas with the conventional pd alias
Printed DataFrame summary: rows x columns

explanations.topic: Installing pandas with pip / pip3
Using uv to create a virtual environment and add pandas
Why pandas is imported as pd
DataFrame vs Series
CSV files and two-dimensional data
pd.read_csv loads a file into a DataFrame
Running with uv run and reading the printed table

hints: Install pandas first: `pip install pandas` (pip3 on Mac/Linux), or `uv init .` then `uv add pandas`.
Put orders.csv from the GitHub repo in the same folder as main.py.
In main.py: `import pandas as pd`, then `df = pd.read_csv('orders.csv')` and `print(df)`.
Run it with `uv run main.py` (or `python main.py`) and look for the 'rows x columns' line at the bottom.
common_mistakes: Running `uv add pandas` before `uv init .`, so there is no project to add it to.
Using `python main.py` outside the uv environment where pandas isn't installed (ModuleNotFoundError).
orders.csv not in the working directory, causing FileNotFoundError.
Typo `pd.readcsv` or `pd.read.csv` instead of `pd.read_csv`.
Downloading the GitHub HTML page instead of the raw CSV file.
steps.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv('orders.csv')
print(df)

steps.title: Load data in Jupyter notebook
steps.instructions: Create notebook.ipynb (Cmd/Ctrl+Shift+P → New Jupyter Notebook); in cell 1 import pandas as pd and read orders.csv with pd.read_csv, then print(df) in cell 2. Pick a Python kernel and run both cells.

targets.caption: First cell: import pandas and load orders.csv

explanations.topic: Why use a Jupyter notebook instead of a .py file for pandas
Creating a notebook via Ctrl/Cmd+Shift+P → New Jupyter Notebook
Installing the VS Code Python extension
Cells run independently; data stays loaded between cells
Run above/below, delete cells, clear outputs

hints: Open the command palette (Ctrl/Cmd+Shift+P), type 'New Jupyter Notebook', then save the file as notebook.ipynb in the same folder as orders.csv.
In the first cell write import pandas as pd and df = pd.read_csv('orders.csv'), then click the run button and choose your Python interpreter as the kernel.
Add a new cell below with print(df) and run only that cell. The table should appear under it with a 'rows x columns' summary.
If the run fails with ModuleNotFoundError, run pip install pandas in the Python environment the kernel uses. If no kernel is offered, install the Python extension from the Extensions pane.
common_mistakes: Saving the notebook in a different folder than orders.csv, which causes FileNotFoundError.
Choosing a kernel or interpreter where pandas isn't installed, which causes ModuleNotFoundError.
Running cell 2 before cell 1, so df is not defined (NameError).
Not having the VS Code Python/Jupyter extension, so 'New Jupyter Notebook' doesn't appear.
Saving the file with a .py extension instead of .ipynb.
steps.run_command: Run cell 1 (pick a Python kernel), then run cell 2
steps.code:
# cell 1
import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv('orders.csv')

# cell 2
print(df)

steps.title: Explore the DataFrame
steps.instructions: In separate notebook cells run `df.head()`, `df.tail()`, `df.info()`, `df.describe()`, `df.columns` and `df.index`. Confirm the entry and column counts that info() reports.

explanations.topic: head() shows the first five rows
tail() shows the last five rows
info(): entries, columns and dtypes
Why text columns show as object dtype
describe() generates descriptive statistics
columns lists column names
index is a RangeIndex (start, stop, step)

hints: Put each command in its own cell and run it so the output appears right below it.
head() and tail() print 5 rows each. info() prints a summary that includes 'RangeIndex: N entries'.
df.columns and df.index are attributes, so leave off the parentheses. df.info() and df.describe() are methods and need ().
common_mistakes: Writing df.columns() or df.index(), which raises 'Index object is not callable'.
Writing df.info or df.describe without (), which shows a bound-method repr instead of the output.
Running these cells before the cell that loads df, which raises NameError: name 'df' is not defined.
Expecting describe() to cover the text columns. By default it only summarises the numeric ones.
steps.run_command: Run each cell in the notebook
steps.code:
df.head()

df.tail()

df.info()

df.describe()

df.columns

df.index

steps.title: Index by column and row
steps.instructions: In your notebook, select a column with df['Country'] and several with df[['Country', 'Product']]. Select rows by position with df.iloc[0] and df.iloc[10]['Country'].

targets.caption: A list of columns returns a DataFrame
Select a row by its position

explanations.topic: Selecting one column returns a pandas Series
Index a DataFrame by column as well as by row
Selecting a list of columns returns a new DataFrame
iloc selects rows by integer position
A row Series can be indexed by position or by column name

hints: Run df.columns first so you know the exact column names to use.
Use single brackets with a column name, df['Country'], to get one column as a Series.
Use double brackets, df[['Country', 'Product']], to get several columns. The inner brackets are a Python list.
For rows, use df.iloc[0]. Chain a column name to get one value, as in df.iloc[10]['Country'].
common_mistakes: Misspelling a column name or getting its case wrong (e.g. 'country'), which raises a KeyError.
Writing df['Country', 'Product'] without the inner list brackets.
Using df[0] instead of df.iloc[0] to get a row.
Calling iloc like a function, df.iloc(0), instead of using square brackets.
Asking for a row position past the end of the data (e.g. iloc[40] on 40 rows), which raises an IndexError.
steps.code:
df.columns
df['Country']
len(df['Country'])
set(df['Country'])
df[['Country', 'Product']]
df.iloc[0]
df.iloc[10]
list(df.iloc[10])
df.iloc[10][0]
df.iloc[10]['Country']

steps.title: Filter rows with conditions
steps.instructions: Filter rows with a boolean mask like df[df['Category'] == 'Electronics'], combine conditions with & and | inside parentheses, and try a numeric filter like df[df['Quantity'] > 2].

explanations.topic: Boolean mask: df[df[col] == value] keeps rows where condition is True
Empty table when filtering the wrong column (Product vs Category)
Use single & (not 'and') with each condition in parentheses
Single pipe | means OR between conditions
Comparison operators >, <, <=, != for numeric filters

hints: Wrap a comparison like df['Category'] == 'Electronics' inside df[...] to keep only matching rows.
To combine two conditions, put each one in its own parentheses and join them with & (and) or | (or).
Numeric columns work with >, <, >=, <=, != e.g. df[df['Quantity'] > 2].
If you get an empty table, check you filtered the right column and the value's exact spelling/case.
common_mistakes: Using Python's 'and'/'or' instead of & and |, which raises 'The truth value of a Series is ambiguous'.
Forgetting parentheses around each condition when combining with & or |, causing operator-precedence errors.
Filtering the wrong column (e.g. Product instead of Category) and getting an empty DataFrame.
Mismatched case or spelling of the value ('electronics' vs 'Electronics') or column name causing KeyError or no rows.
Comparing a numeric column to a string like '2' instead of the number 2.

steps.title: Use string and isin filters
steps.instructions: Filter with .str.startswith('A') and .str.endswith('a') on a text column, then use .isin([...]) and negate it with ~.

targets.caption: isin keeps rows whose value is in the list

explanations.topic: Using .str string methods to filter a column
String matching is case-sensitive (endswith 'A' vs 'a')
isin replaces long combined OR conditions
~ operator reverses a boolean condition

hints: Call string methods through the .str accessor on a column, e.g. df['col'].str.startswith(...), and wrap the result in df[...] to filter.
Matching is case-sensitive: names ending in a lowercase letter need endswith('a'), not 'A'.
isin takes a list: df[df['Country'].isin(['USA', 'Sweden', 'Brazil'])].
To get rows NOT in the list, put ~ before the condition: df[~df['Country'].isin([...])].
common_mistakes: Calling df['CustomerName'].startswith('A') without .str, which raises an AttributeError.
Using uppercase 'A' with endswith and getting an empty result because matching is case-sensitive.
Passing separate arguments to isin, e.g. isin('USA', 'Sweden'), instead of a single list.
Using 'not' or '!' instead of ~ to negate a pandas boolean Series.
Forgetting the outer df[...] and only seeing a True/False Series instead of filtered rows.

steps.title: Update data with loc
steps.instructions: In notebook.ipynb, update values with df.loc[condition, 'column'] = new_value (e.g. rename 'USA' to 'United States' in Country), then uppercase a column with df['Country'] = df['Country'].str.upper(). Run the cells and check the printed column.

targets.caption: Locate rows by condition, then pick a column to assign
Uppercase every value in a column

explanations.topic: loc locates by label/condition vs iloc by integer position
loc with a condition returns a DataFrame since multiple rows may match
Adding a column after the comma lets you assign new values
Condition-based update changes all matching rows at once
Vectorised string methods via .str to transform a whole column

hints: Use df.loc[condition, 'ColumnName'] = new_value; the condition selects the rows and the label selects the column.
The condition looks like df['Country'] == 'USA'. Put it inside .loc[...] and add a comma before the column name.
To transform a whole column, assign it back to itself: df['Country'] = df['Country'].str.upper().
Re-run a filter afterwards (e.g. df[df['Country'] == 'United States']) to confirm the change.
common_mistakes: Using chained indexing like df[df['Country']=='USA']['Country'] = ... which triggers SettingWithCopyWarning and doesn't update df
Misspelling the column label (e.g. 'ProductName' instead of 'Product'), which creates a new column instead of updating
Calling df['Country'].upper() without .str, which raises AttributeError
Forgetting to assign the result back with df['Country'] = ..., so the column stays unchanged
Filtering for 'USA' after uppercasing/renaming and being confused by empty results
steps.code:
df.loc[df['CustomerName'] == 'Anna ...']
df.loc[df['CustomerName'] == 'Anna ...', 'Product'] = 'Tim'
df.loc[df['CustomerName'] == 'Anna ...']

df.loc[df['Country'] == 'USA', 'Country'] = 'United States'
df[df['Country'] == 'USA']
df[df['Country'] == 'United States']

df['Country'] = df['Country'].str.upper()
df['Country']

steps.title: Drop rows and clean data
steps.instructions: Remove a row with `df = df.drop(<index>)`, check with `df.tail()`, then reload the CSV. Use `df.dropna()`, `df.fillna({...}, inplace=True)` and `df.rename(columns={...}, inplace=True)`.

targets.caption: Drop a row by index and reassign df
Confirm the dropped row is gone

explanations.topic: drop() removes a row by its index label
dropna() removes rows containing null/NA values
fillna replaces missing values instead of removing rows
inplace=True modifies the existing DataFrame vs returning a new one
Renaming columns with rename(columns={...})

hints: Removing a row uses df.drop with the row's index label, and you need to reassign the result to df.
Use df.tail() to confirm the row is gone, then reload the CSV with pd.read_csv so later steps start from clean data.
fillna and rename accept a dict, like {'OrderID': 0} and columns={'OrderID': 'Order ID'}. Pass inplace=True so df itself changes.
Print df after renaming. The header should now show 'Order ID' with a space.
common_mistakes: Calling df.drop(39) without assigning it back (df = df.drop(39)), so the row is not actually removed.
Running df.drop(39) twice, which raises KeyError because index 39 no longer exists.
Writing inplace=True and also assigning the result (df = df.fillna(..., inplace=True)), which sets df to None.
Misspelling the column key in rename (for example 'OrderId'), which silently renames nothing.
Expecting df.dropna() alone to change df. Without reassignment or inplace=True it returns a new DataFrame.
steps.code:
df = df.drop(39)
df.tail()

# reload the CSV
df = pd.read_csv('data.csv')

df.dropna()
df.fillna({'OrderID': 0}, inplace=True)
df.rename(columns={'OrderID': 'Order ID'}, inplace=True)
df

steps.title: Analyze, group and save
steps.instructions: Run df['Country'].value_counts(), df.groupby('Country')['Price'].sum() and df.sort_values('Price', ascending=False). Save with df.to_csv('new_file.csv', index=False).

targets.caption: Save the modified DataFrame to a new CSV

explanations.topic: value_counts counts occurrences of each value in a column
groupby works like SQL GROUP BY, aggregating price per country
sort_values with ascending=False sorts descending
to_csv saves the DataFrame; index=True/False controls writing the index

hints: Each of these is one line on df; put each in its own cell and run it.
value_counts is called on a single column: df['Country'].value_counts().
For grouping: df.groupby('Country')['Price'].sum(). For sorting: df.sort_values('Price', ascending=False).
Save with df.to_csv('new_file.csv', index=False) and look for the new file next to your notebook.
common_mistakes: Calling value_counts on the whole DataFrame instead of one column.
Summing a Price column that is still text (strings with '$'), which concatenates or errors instead of adding numbers.
Leaving ascending at its default True and getting the cheapest items first.
Writing df.to_csv without index=False, which adds an extra unnamed index column to the file.
Column name typos or case mismatches like 'country' vs 'Country' causing KeyError.
steps.code:
df['Country'].value_counts()

df.groupby('Country')['Price'].sum()

df.sort_values('Price', ascending=False)

df.to_csv('new_file.csv', index=False)
